findings.question: q-trigonometry-laws-of-sines-and-cosines-0018
findings.quote: This treats an obtuse cosine as positive in the subtraction term. Both cosine values have magnitude one-half. Check their signs before comparing the squares.
findings.problem: This note does not explain choosing the first triangle as having the longer third side. Using positive one-half for both cosines gives 25+64-40=49 for both third-side squares, so the described mistake produces the equal-length choice instead.
findings.fix: Describe reversing the cosine signs: using -1/2 for 60 degrees and +1/2 for 120 degrees makes the first side appear longer. Remind the student to check each cosine sign.

findings.question: q-trigonometry-laws-of-sines-and-cosines-0019
findings.problem: The opening asserts that this triangle exists, but these measurements cannot form a triangle: b sin A = 10(1/2) = 5 exceeds a = 4, or equivalently sin B = 5/4. The intended error-spotting solution correctly discovers nonexistence, contradicting the factual premise.
findings.fix: Begin with "A student checks whether a triangle ABC can have a=4, b=10, and A=30 degrees" and retain the proposed calculation steps.

findings.question: q-trigonometry-laws-of-sines-and-cosines-0020
findings.quote: This assumes the supplementary angle makes the angle sum too large. That can happen in SSA problems. Check each possible sum against $180^\circ$.
findings.problem: Rejecting only the supplementary angle would leave the principal angle of about 45.6 degrees, whose sum with 30 degrees is 75.6 degrees. That mistake gives one triangle, not the zero-triangle choice this note is meant to explain.
findings.fix: Explain a mistake that actually gives zero, such as swapping the sides to obtain sin R = 10/(7 sin 30 degrees) > 1. Say why the swapped setup looks tempting and advise checking opposite side-angle pairs.
